Brief facts of the case
1.
In brief the case of the prosecution is that on 13.07.2007 at about 12:15 p.m, Food Inspector Sanjiv
Kumar Gupta and Field Assistant Sh. Brahma Nand under the supervision and directions of Sdm /
Lha Sh. M. K. Dwivedi visited the premises of M/s Needs Departmental Store, S. No. G1/28,
Sector11, Rohini, Delhi110085 where accused Rajesh Kumar who was the Vendorcum Proprietor
was found present conducting the business of various food articles including Lal Mirch Kutti, for
sale for human consumption and in compliance of the provisions of the Prevention of Food
Adulteration Act, 1954 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 (hereinafter referred to
as the Act & Rules) the Food Inspector collected / purchased the sample of Lal Mirch Kutti from
accused Rajesh Kumar.

2. During the course of investigation it was revealed that Sh. Rajesh Kumar S/o Sh. Rishi Parkash
Gupta was the vendorcumproprietor of M/s Needs Departmental Store and thus the Incharge of
and responsible for the day to day conduct of the business of the said shop.

3.  It is further the prosecution's case that the sample of Lal Mirch Kutti purchased from accused Rajesh Kumar was sent to Public Analyst for analysis and as per the report of Public Analyst, the sample was misbranded because of complete violation of Rule 32 of PFA Rules, 1955.

However,
Mirch Kutti was found conforming to standards.

4. After the complaint was filed, the accused was summoned vide order dated 02.01.2008.
5.

Notice for violation of provision of Section 2 (ix) (k) of PFA Act, 1954 r/w Rule 32 of PFA Rules,
1955 which is punishable u/s 16 (1) (a) of PFA Act 1954 r/w Section 7 of the PFA Act was framed against the accused vide order dated 23.10.2009 to which accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
6. Statement of the accused U/s 313 Cr. P.C. was recorded on 22.08.2013 wherein the accused claimed himself to be innocent.
Accused himself examined as DW1 in his defence.

A brief scrutiny of the evidence recorded in the matter is as under:
7. PW1

Sh. Sanjiv Kumar Gupta deposed that on 13.07.2007, he alongwith Sh. Brahamnand, FA and other staff under the supervision and direction of SDM/LHA, SH. M.K. Dwivedi visited M/s Da vs . Rajesh Kumar Page 1 Of 10 on 13 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85411611/
2

Needs Departmental Store, Sl. No. G1/28, Sector11, Rohini, Delhi, where accused Rajesh Kumar was found conducting the business of the food articles and sale of spices including Lal Mirch Kutti ,
a food article for human consumption for sale.

He deposed that he disclosed his identity and intention for purchasing the sample of Lal Mirch Kutti available in sealed packets without any label declaration stated to be of same lot and ready for sale, for analysis, to which accused agreed.
He deposed that before taking the sample, he tried his best to procure some public witnesses by requesting some neighborers, customers and passersby etc. to join the sample proceedings.
But as none agreed for the same, FA Brahamanand joined as witness.
He deposed that at about 12:15 pm, he purchased 6 sealed packets of Lal Mirch Kutti bearing no label declaration on payment of Rs. 150/ vide vendor's receipt Ex.PW1/A.

He deposed that he divided the sample into three equal parts by putting two originally sealed packets of Lal Mirch Kutti in one counterpart and each counterpart containing the sample of Lal Mirch Kutti was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed according to PFA Act and Rules.
He deposed that LHA slips bearing his code number and signature were affixed on each counterpart.
He deposed that vendor signatures were obtained on LHA Slip on each counterpart of the sample in such a manner that a portion of his signature were on the wrapper as well as on the LHA Slips.
He deposed that Notice in Form VI Ex. PW1/B was prepared at the spot and copy of it was given to the accused as per his endorsement at potion A to A bearing his signature at point A.
He deposed that Panchnama Ex.PW1/C was prepared.
He deposed that accused also made endorsement that the sample packets were of same lot.
He deposed that vendor also furnished his statement Ex.PW1/D that he is the proprietor of the said shop.

He deposed that all these documents Ex.PW1/A and Ex.PW1/C were read over and explained to the accused in Hindi and after understanding the same accused signed at point A and witness signed at Point B and then he signed at point C respectively.

He deposed that the one counterpart of the sample with a copy of Memo VII in intact condition was deposited with the PA on 16.07.2007 i.e. next working day vide receipt Ex.PW1/E and a Memo VII in a sealed packed separately.
He deposed that all the copies of Memo in Form VII bear the seal impression with which sample were sealed.

He deposed that the two counterparts of the sample alongwith two copies of memo of Form VII in a sealed packet were deposited in intact condition with LHA on 16.07.2007 i.e. next working day vide receipt Ex.PW1/F bearing his signature at point A with the intimation that one counterpart of the sample has already been deposited in intact condition with the PA.
He deposed that all the copies of memo of Form VII bore the same seal impression with which the sample in question was sealed.
He deposed that the PA Report Ex.PW1/G was received according to which, the sample was misbranded as there was complete violation of Rule 32.
He deposed that however, Lal Mirch Kutti was found conforming to standard, as mentioned therein at portion X.
He deposed that during investigation, he sent a letter Ex.PW1/H to STO Ward No. 63 and as per its reply at portion A, no such firm was found registered with Sales Tax.

He deposed that he also inquired from the office vide memo Ex.PW1/1 that any previous warning was issued to the accused as per department policy and it was informed that no previous warning was issued to the accused for violation of Rule 32 and copy of order No. 5/7 Ex.PW1/J was provided by the department.
He deposed that during investigation, accused was found proprietor of the shop.

He deposed that on completion of the investigation, the complete case file alongwith all statutory documents were sent through LHA/ SDM to the then Director (PFA), Shri N. Balachandaran who after going through the case file, applied his mind and gave his consent for prosecution Ex.PW1/K,

3 which bears his signature at point A.
He deposed that the complaint Ex.PW1/L was filed in Court by him bearing signatures at point A.

He deposed that the intimation letter Ex.PW1/M bearing the signature of SDM/LHA at point A was sent alongwith the copy of PA Report by registered post to accused as mentioned therein which were not received back undelivered.

He deposed that the photocopy of the Postal Registration Receipt is Ex.PW1/N bearing the relevant entry at point A.
8.
During his cross examination he admitted that on the day of sampling, the policy of the department not to prosecute for first violation of Rule 32 was in existence.
He denied the suggestion that accused was discriminated by not issuing warning for first violation of Rule 32 by the department.
9. PW2 Sh. Brahma Nand, Field Assistant and PW3 Sh. M.K. Dwivedi, the then SDM/LHA have deposed on the same lines as deposed by PW1 in his examination in chief.
This so far is the prosecution evidence in the matter.

12. In his defence, the accused examined himself as DW1 u/s 315 Cr.P.C.
13.

DW1 Sh. Rajesh Kumar deposed that he was running a petty shop at the ground floor of H. NO.
G1/28, Sector 11, Rohini, Delhi85, he was residing at the first floor of the same premises.
He deposed that his shop is under the name and style of M/s Needs Departmental Store.
He deposed that he is still running the same.
He deposed that he used to sell packed items for daily needs like biscuits, namkeen, dahi etc. at his shop.
He deposed that he used to grind the spices of the customers on their orders and used to charge price for the same.
14. During his cross examination he admitted that at the time of sampling Lal Mirch Kutti was lying in sealed polypackets of 200 gms each without having any label or declaration.
The customers used to bring their ungrinded spices for grinding the same in loose/open condition but on their instructions he used to packed them in small packets after grinding the same.
He told the Food Inspector that the sample commodity was not meant for sale but he insisted for giving the sample to him.
He did not call any member of Market Association or any respectable member of the society to inform them that the Food Inspector is lifting the sample of the commodity which was not meant for sale.
He denied the suggestion that sample commodity was not given to him by any person for the purpose of grinding and it was stored by him for sale to general public/customers.
15. This so far is the evidence in the matter.
16. I have heard the arguments advanced at bar by the Ld. defence counsel as also the Ld. SPP for complainant.
I have also carefully gone through the entire record including the evidence recorded in the matter and perused the documents placed on record by the prosecution in this case.

17. After carefully applying my mind to the rival contentions raised at bar as well as on careful scrutiny of the material on record, I am of the considered opinion that the accused is entitled to be acquitted in the present case.
Reason for Decision.

It is urged by Ld. Counsel for the accused that the sample lifted from accused was found conforming to standards and was only found deficient for compliance of labelling rules as provided under Rule 32 of PFA Rules.

The policy of giving warning for first time violation of labelling conditions/requirements was in force at the time of taking sample and the prosecution could be launched only if the defaulter continue with default after the warning.
The department instead of launching the prosecution of accused ought to have brought the default to the notice of accused by way of sending written warning in terms of policy No. F6 (228)/85/ENF/PFA.

Reliance is placed upon judgment of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in M/s Pepsi Food Pvt. Ltd & Anr Vs. State and Anr.
2012 (2) FAC 428 by Ld. Counsel for accused.
19.

Pepsi Food Pvt. Ltd & Anr Vs. State and Anr.
2012 (2) FAC 428
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In order to properly appreciate the contention of learned counsel for the accused, it would be appropriate to reproduce the relevant policy relied upon by the Counsel for accused.

It reads thus:
"2. It would be noted from the perusal of the above Rule that an elaborate procedure has been prescribed for labelling sealed contents indicating therein the code number date of packing etc.

However, it has been noticed that in quite a few cases contents of the sealed article of food was found conforming to the standard prescribed under the Rules, whereas the labelling done on the container or the packet was deficient in certain respect and was not in conformity with the provision contained in rule 32 of the PFA Rules, 1955.

After detailed discussion on the subject, it was appreciated that in case the contents of the sealed packets or container conform to the standard laid down under the PFA Rules, deficiency with regard to Rule 32 which pertains to the particulars of the labelling on the container or packet, was only a technical ofence,
though it attracted Rule 32 and there was breach of this Rule in some respect in the course of packing the article of food.

In such cases there was unanimous view during the course of discussion that the party effected may be given a written warning drawing his attention to Rule 32 which provides for labelling particulars to be exhibited on the sampled Tin or the packet and in case the practice is repeated after a written warning to the party concerned, the party committing the offence second time should be prosecuted.
However, this could not apply in case where the contents of the sealed packed or container are not conforming to the prescribed standard and hence are adulterated.
In such cases, prosecution would be launched both for adulteration and for breach of Rules 32.
After the Secretary (Medical), as the consenting Authority, has approved the above proposal all the pending cases would be disposed of accordingly."

20. In the matter S. S. Gokul Krishnan & Ors Vs. State through Food Inspector Govt. of NCT of Delhi, 2009 (1) FAC 132 wherein the above policy was subject matter of dispute, Hon'ble High Court of Delhi observed thus:
"27.

entities.text: S. S. Gokul Krishnan & Ors Vs. State through Food Inspector Govt. of NCT of Delhi, 2009 (1) FAC 132
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The alleged offence of violation of Rule 32 (f) and (i) was found to have been committed in the year 2005.
At the relevant time department policy No. F6 (228)/85/ENF/P.F.A. was in force and the said policy was cancelled, modified or withdrawn vide order no. 5/07 dated 14.09.2007.

As per the said policy, cases of Da vs . Rajesh Kumar Page 1 Of 10 on 13 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85411611/
5 breach of Rule 32, since pertained to the particulars of the labelling on the container or packet, were technical offences, the party affected was to be given a written warning drawing its attention to Rule 32, which required of date, month and year of manufacturing to be exhibited on the labels affixed on tin or the packet.
It was only if the violation was repeated after a written warning, the party committing the offence second time had to be prosecuted.
As per this policy, pending cases pertaining to breach of Rule 32 being of technical nature were decided to be disposed of accordingly.

28. It is not the case of the prosecution that petitioners were given warning by way of a notice drawing their attention to Rule 32 which provided for particulars to be exhibited on the sampled tin or the packet, and it was a case of second breach of Rule 32, i.e in other words the offence was committed for the second time and therefore,
the petitioners was liable to be prosecuted.
29.
The policy being in force at the relevant time should have been adhered to by the department before it decided to file a complaint in the court for offences under Section 7/16 of the PFA Act.
The petitioners are therefore within their rights to seek protection under the said policy which was in existence at the relevant time."
21. In the instant case, the sample conformed to the standards but was found wanting with regard to compliance of Rule 32 of PFA Rules.
It tantamounts to only a technical offence.
At the time of lifting of sample i.e. 13.07.2007 the policy no. F6 (228)/85/ENF/PFA was in force.

The testimony of PW1,
Food Inspector, also reveals that no previous warning was issued to the accused for violation of Rule 32 of PFA Rules.
Thus, the facts of the present case are squarely covered by the ratio of judgment of S. S. Gokul Krishnan (supra).

The said decision was also followed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in M/s Pepsi Food Pvt. Ltd (supra), M/s Hindustan Lever Ltd Vs State of NCT of Delhi & Ors. 2011 (1)
FAC 183 & M/s Gupta Tea Traders Vs. State 2012 (2) FAC 415.
22.

entities.text:
Hindustan Lever Ltd Vs State of NCT of Delhi & Ors. 2011 (1)
FAC 183
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Gupta Tea Traders Vs. State 2012 (2) FAC 415
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In view of the aforesaid discussions, I am of the view that the accused was entitled to benefit of written warning drawing his attention to the default committed by him in respect of labelling requirements, in terms of the prevalent policy no. F6 (228)/85/ENF/PFA.
But no such warning was given to him.

So, the accused Rajesh Kumar is acquitted for 16 (1) (a) of PFA Act 1954 r/w Section 7 of the PFA Act for violation of Section 2 (ix) (k) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Rule 32 of PFA Rules,
1955.
